voice_profile: Brisk, comic third-person narration in close focus on one young adventurer at a time. It works through quick dialogue tags ('snarled', 'sweetly', 'moralized'), slangy period banter ('old bean', 'keep her end up', 'a dirty trick!'), and wry narrative asides that undercut the heroics: Tuppence admiring her own ingenuity, or Tommy reasoning 'in his usual slow and steady way'. Suspense comes from short paragraphs, dashes, trailing ellipses and abrupt chapter-end cliffhangers. Characters are often 'telling the truth' in ways others misread. Menace is conveyed through physical tells such as shifty eyes, purpling faces and a sibilant voice, and through ironic political epigram.
book_context: A 1920s thriller built on the joint venture of Tommy and Tuppence. Chapters alternate between their separate adventures and end on cliffhangers. Recurring mechanisms include accidental truth-telling that works as a bluff; names dropped casually that become clues ('Jane Finn', 'Rita', the clerk 'Brown'); and the faceless 'Mr. Brown', always suspected to be an unnoticed person present in the room. The approaching date of the 29th drives the plot. Chapter II plants the clues that Carter and Tuppence later decode in IV and VI. Chapter VIII plants the date, the conspirators' faces, Jane's mysterious incapacity and the recess hiding-place, all of which pay off in XVI, XVII and the climax in XXVI–XXVII. Abridgment must keep these plants without explaining them early.

verbatim.purpose: Chapter-closing punchline; Ch. III opens directly on its aftermath.

essential: Tuppence is accosted in St. James's Park by a big, clean-shaven, heavy-jowled man with small shifty eyes. He says he overheard her in Lyons' and followed her. She instinctively distrusts him but is unafraid.
His card reads Mr. Edward Whittington, Esthonia Glassware Co., with an eleven o'clock appointment the next morning. Keep her terrier-like shake and the 'adventures have begun' resolve.
She wires Tommy, using his retained pencil: 'Don't put in advertisement. Will explain to-morrow.' Keep the ninepence-versus-five-shillings economy.
At the office a middle-aged clerk at a desk in the small outer office shows her through a 'Private' door. Keep the outer office's existence and the clerk's ordinariness.

The offer: £100 down plus expenses for about three months at Madame Colombier's pensionnat in Paris, as Whittington's ward. Conditions are no communication with friends and absolute secrecy. He suggests she pass as an American because of her accent.

She objects that the terms are too liberal. He says he is paying for intelligence, presence of mind and discretion not to ask questions. She insists the deal is 'both or neither' with her partner Beresford.

Asked her name, she blurts 'Jane Finn' to spare the archdeacon. Do NOT explain here where the name came from; Ch. III reveals that Tommy mentioned it. Whittington's face turns purple with rage and dismay.

Tuppence bluffs by telling literal truths: Rita knows nothing of her; she knows 'very little'; it might be her own name or chance. Each answer deepens his unease. Keep the double-bluff logic and his 'How much do you know? And how much do you want?'
She proposes 'a little something down' and denies blackmail ('payment of services in advance'). Whittington shows grudging admiration.
The clerk brings a 'telephone message'. Whittington frowns, dismisses him as Brown, abruptly gives her £50 and tells her to return tomorrow. Do not hint that the clerk matters.
Whittington becomes suspiciously genial again, which gives Tuppence a faint misgiving. She leaves elated and takes a taxi to surprise Tommy.
optional: Paragraph 1–2 detail of her first assumption about his motives can be compressed to one sentence.
The post-office pen ('spiky pen and thick, black treacle') and Tommy's club-subscription aside can be cut, but keep the wire itself.
Buns at the baker's and the cubicle reflection can be reduced. If buns are cut, also drop the 'supper of buns' reference in p90, or keep both.
Her walk to the end of the street to avoid looking over-eager, and taking the stairs rather than the lift, can be cut.
Tuppence's aside about her father and the 'gay deceiver' (p46) can be cut.
Some repetitions of 'quit fooling' and 'you insist on misjudging me' in the haggling (p91–97) can be trimmed, keeping one round of bluff and counter-bluff.
The au revoir exchange can be shortened, but keep his 'clever and charming young lady' and her misgiving.

continuity_checks: The clerk is called Brown only once, in Whittington's dismissal, with no narrative emphasis.
The 'Jane Finn' name is not explained as coming from Tommy.
Rita is mentioned by Whittington, not Tuppence.
The amount handed over is fifty (£), in notes that include five-pound notes, consistent with the taxi line.
The wire text is preserved so Ch. III's 'You're not going to put that thing in after all?' makes sense.
Tommy's pencil is retained by Tuppence.
risks: The haggling dialogue is the comic core. Over-trimming it may lose the escalating truth-as-bluff logic, so keep at least three of her truthful replies.

verbatim.text: deciding that the mention of “Mr. Brown” was not a request for an individual, but in all probability a password used by the gang.
verbatim.purpose: Tommy's slow, steady reasoning; frames the password that matters again in Ch. XVI.

verbatim.text: But, all the same, it is possible that he is among us now....” He looked round him again, and again that expression of fear swept over the group. Each man seemed eyeing his neighbour doubtfully.
verbatim.purpose: Core statement of the Mr. Brown motif: the leader may be anyone present.

verbatim.text: They are honest men--and that is their value to us. It is curious--but you cannot make a revolution without honest men.
verbatim.purpose: Ironic political epigram; the 'honest men' idea underlies Tommy's later strategy.

verbatim.text: “Every revolution has had its honest men. They are soon disposed of afterwards.”
verbatim.purpose: Sinister punchline; its exact wording carries the menace.

verbatim.text: But Tommy heard no more. A crashing blow descended on his head, and all was darkness.

essential: Tommy enters the filthy house and climbs the stairs. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password, and that entering the meeting room risks a further password or proof of identity.
He hides in the curtained recess opposite the meeting-room door, which also overlooks the stairs. Keep its position and the rents in the curtain that let him watch.

He watches the arrivals. A brutish criminal answers 'Fourteen' to the bearded, precise-voiced German chairing the table ('Your number, comrade?' / 'Correct'), and Tommy is glad he did not walk in. Then come an Irish Sinn Feiner, a shabby city-clerk type, a working man whose face is vaguely familiar, and an exquisitely dressed, commanding man whose face is also familiar but unnamed.
Tommy reflects on how far-reaching and strange this chain of links under Mr. Brown is.

The last arrival is a small, pale man with a hissing voice and Slavonic cheekbones. His eyes seem to burn through the curtain and make Tommy shiver; he likens him to a venomous snake. He is received with deference as 'Number One'. Do NOT name him or hint at his public identity.
Number One asks for Mr. Brown. The German says Brown cannot attend in person, leaving the sentence oddly unfinished. Number One suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye each other in fear.

The door is shut. Tommy removes his shoes, fails to open the locked door, carefully restores the handle, then gets into the adjoining bedroom. He draws the rusty bolt of the communicating door and can hear through a portière but not see.

Overheard business, kept in summary: Irish money and ammunition, with money routed via Irish Americans and 'Mr. Potter' (an American voice notes waning sympathy); a loan to an English newspaper with Moscow denial; union reports (miners satisfactory, hold back railways).
The date is the 29th, set by the Labour leaders, who must believe it their own show. Include Number One's 'honest men' remarks.
Clymes 'must go'; Number Fourteen will see to it, wearing gloves with a housebreaker's prints, and he relishes blood in the streets.

The German admits the honest Labour leaders may not strike, because public opinion favours the Government. A certain document would assure success, but they do not have it. Perhaps only 'a girl' knows where it is; 'This case is different'. As the German begins to say where she is, Tommy is struck down from behind. The attacker is unseen.
optional: Description of the grimy wallpaper and cobwebs can be compressed to one phrase.
The detailed recess measurements ('two feet deep and three feet wide') can be cut, but keep 'recess' and 'curtain'.
Paragraph 4's extended risk deliberation can be shortened to one or two sentences.
Tommy's 'If that isn't a Hun, I'm a Dutchman!' aside can be shortened, but keep the German identification.
The slow handle-turning sequence (p34–35, p38) can be heavily compressed. Keep: tried the door, found it locked, restored the handle quietly, and his bulldog tenacity.
The Belfast quip by the commanding man (p56) can be cut, along with the American voice's specifics, keeping only the money-routing gist.
The A.S.E. and miners/railways details can be reduced to 'reports from the unions'.
Nothing removed should orphan 'Number Fourteen': keep both his arrival number and his Clymes assignment, or reference him clearly.
